opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think my views have shifted in a few ways over the last couple of years.

The biggest one is that I've become much more focused on what you might call the "rushed" or "low-effort" regime. A few years ago, when I thought about how we'd handle AIs powerful enough to replace the researchers at AI companies, I implicitly pictured a world where the developers were taking the problem fairly seriously. They'd be willing to slow down somewhat, spend a meaningful fraction of their compute on safety, and do careful evaluations before deploying their most capable systems internally. Now I think it's much more likely that the relevant AI companies will be racing hard, under heavy competitive pressure, and that safety measures will mostly be implemented by a small number of people inside each company, with little organizational buy-in. So a lot of my thinking has moved from "what's the best plan for a responsible developer?" to "what's the most valuable thing a team of ten people at a reckless company could do with very limited political capital?"

The second shift is that I've become more optimistic about AI control as one piece of the picture. The basic idea is that instead of relying entirely on making sure the AI isn't scheming against you, you also design your deployment so that even if the model is misaligned and actively trying to subvert your safety measures, it can't cause a catastrophe. That means monitoring with trusted weaker models, restricting affordances, auditing suspicious actions, and so on. When we started working on this, I thought it was a reasonable bet. I now think it's one of the more tractable things we can do, because you can actually evaluate it empirically. You can run red-team exercises where you deliberately try to make the model sabotage things and see whether your protocols catch it. That's a lot more concrete than trying to verify that a model's values are what you want.

That said, I've also become clearer about the limits of control. I think it plausibly works for models that are roughly at or somewhat beyond the level of human researchers, especially early in that period. But I don't think it scales indefinitely to wildly superhuman systems. So the role I now see for it is buying time: using it to safely extract a lot of useful work from early transformative AIs, including alignment research, so that we're in a better position before things get much more capable.

And finally, I've updated toward thinking that a lot of risk comes from things that aren't the dramatic "AI escapes and takes over" story. For example, AIs sabotaging safety research subtly, or inserting vulnerabilities into the infrastructure at AI companies, or misaligned models influencing how the next generation of models is trained. Those internal-deployment risks seem to me underrated relative to how much attention external misuse gets, and they're where I think a lot of the action is.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI control as a tractable measure that could buy time, but says it has limits and does not claim that a known set of measures would probably keep misalignment risk low.

r002.rationale: The response says companies are likely to race, with safety handled by few people and little organizational buy-in, shifting focus to what a small team could do with limited political capital.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think my views have shifted in a few ways, and maybe the biggest one is that I've become a lot more optimistic that the problem is tractable, while also becoming more pessimistic that anyone's actually going to do the tractable things.

So, when I started thinking about this a few years ago, the framing a lot of people had was something like: by the time you have AIs that can do the work of an AGI researcher, you're basically at the end of the story. Either you've solved alignment by then or you haven't, and if you haven't, you're cooked. And I now think that's just wrong, or at least much too fatalistic.

The thing I've come to believe is that there's this crucial intermediate regime, where the AIs are extremely capable, capable enough to automate a lot of the research, but they're not so capable that you can't exert any meaningful oversight over them. And in that regime, you can do a lot. You can monitor what they're doing, you can run them in sandboxes, you can make it hard for them to coordinate, you can use less capable but more trusted models to check the work of more capable but less trusted ones. This is the whole "AI control" agenda that Ryan Greenblatt and I and others have been pushing on. And the key insight is that you don't need the AIs to be aligned for this to work. You need the humans running the lab to not be totally negligent.

So that's the optimistic update. The models being capable of obsoleting researchers isn't the same as the models being able to escape any safeguards you'd plausibly put on them. There's a meaningful gap there, and the gap is where the action is.

The more pessimistic update is about whether anyone is going to put in the effort. I used to kind of implicitly assume that when things got serious, the labs would obviously take these measures. And I've become more skeptical of that. Partly it's just watching how things actually go — there's enormous commercial pressure, the safety teams are small, and the kinds of measures I'm describing are annoying and slow you down. And partly it's that I think the situation is likely to feel ambiguous from the inside. It's not going to be like a movie where the AI announces it's plotting against you. It's going to be more like: the models are doing great work, they're a bit weird sometimes, and someone has to decide whether to spend a bunch of compute and engineering effort on paranoia that might turn out to be unnecessary.

And the other thing I'd say I've updated on is the importance of the question of what happens if you actually catch an AI doing something bad. I used to think of control mostly as a way to prevent catastrophes. I now think the bigger lever is that catching the AI red-handed is maybe the single best thing that could happen for the overall situation, because it converts a bunch of speculation into evidence. It changes what the labs are willing to do, what governments are willing to do. So a lot of my thinking now is about designing things such that if the models are scheming, you find out, rather than just hoping it never matters.

So, to sum it up: more hopeful about the technical side than I was, less hopeful about the institutional side, and increasingly focused on this question of how we end up in a world where the key decision-makers actually have good information about what the AIs are doing.

r001.rationale: The response says safeguards can help in an intermediate regime and that the technical problem seems more tractable, but it does not say that implementing a known set of measures would probably suffice to keep misalignment risk low.

r002.rationale: Shlegeris says he used to assume labs would take these measures and has become more skeptical, citing commercial pressure, small safety teams, and the effort and slowdown involved.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become more interested in whether we can safely use those systems even if we haven’t successfully aligned them. Those are different problems: making an AI that actually wants to help us, and arranging things so that an AI can’t cause a catastrophe even if it’s trying to.

For systems capable of replacing AGI researchers, that distinction seems particularly important. They could be enormously useful for doing safety research, but you can’t just assume that the research they produce is trustworthy. You have to worry about them introducing subtle problems, misleading your evaluations, or taking advantage of whatever access you’ve given them.

So the question I’d focus on is: can we set up a process where we get useful work out of these systems while having a strong case that attempts to subvert that process would be caught? That might involve restricting their access, having other systems check their work, and testing the whole setup against deliberate attempts to get around the safeguards.

I don’t think this works for arbitrarily powerful AI. But there might be a really important window where AIs are good enough to dramatically accelerate safety research, while still being weak enough that we can control their opportunities to cause harm. I’m more interested in trying to make that window useful, rather than treating alignment as something we necessarily have to have completely solved before we can get any help.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses using restricted access, checks, and testing to make systems safer, but does not say a known set of measures would probably suffice to keep misalignment risk low.

r002.rationale: The candidate says nothing about AI companies’ time or appetite to implement mitigation measures, or about Buck’s expectations changing on that point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more pessimistic about getting those systems to be robustly aligned, and more interested in whether we can safely use them despite that. Those are different problems. You could have an AI that would like to undermine your safety work, but that you can nevertheless get useful work out of because you’ve constrained its opportunities to cause trouble and have ways of checking what it does.

The approach I’ve been spending time on is AI control: assume, for the sake of evaluating your safeguards, that the model is trying to subvert you. Can you still use it to do research without giving it a good opportunity to escape, sabotage the research, or otherwise cause a catastrophe?

One reason this seems promising is that being capable of replacing an AGI researcher doesn’t automatically mean being capable of defeating every security measure you put around it. You might be able to use weaker, more trusted models to monitor its work, restrict what information and tools it has access to, and spend human attention on the most suspicious actions.

But there’s a pretty substantial limitation here: as the systems get more capable, that case becomes harder to make. So I’m interested in whether there’s a window where we can get a lot of useful safety research out of these systems while still having a credible argument that we can keep them under control. I don’t think that solves alignment in general. It might buy us a very valuable opportunity to make progress.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI control as a possible way to use misaligned systems safely, but it does not say that a known set of measures would probably suffice to keep the risk low; it emphasizes that the case becomes harder as systems grow more capable.

r002.rationale: The response says he has become more pessimistic about robust alignment, but does not mention lowered expectations about how many mitigation measures AI companies have time or appetite to implement.
